Title: Bye Bye Perspective API: Lessons for Measurement Infrastructure in NLP, CSS and LLM Evaluation
Text:
Bye Bye PERSPECTIVE API:
Lessons for Measurement Infrastructure in NLP, CSS and LLM Evaluation
David Hartmann1,2, Manuel Tonneau1,3, Angelie Kraft1, LK Seiling1,
Dimitri Staufer2, Pieter Delobelle4,5, Jan Fillies6, Anna Ricarda Luther7,8,
Jan Batzner1,9,10, Mareike Lisker11,12
1Weizenbaum Institute, 2TU Berlin, 3University of Oxford, 4KU Leuven, 5Pleias,
6Freie Universität Berlin, 7University of Bremen, 8ifib research,
9TU Munich, 10Munich Center for Machine Learning, 11HTW Berlin, 12University of Hamburg
Correspondence: d.hartmann@tu-berlin.de
Abstract
The closure of PERSPECTIVE API at the end
of 2026 discards what has functioned as the
de facto standard for automated toxicity mea-
surement in NLP, CSS, and LLM evaluation re-
search. We document the structural dependence
that the communities built on this single pro-
prietary tool and discuss how this dependence
caused epistemic problems that have affected—
and will likely continue to affect—collective
research efforts. PERSPECTIVE’s model was pe-
riodically updated without versioning or disclo-
sure, its annotation structure reflected a single
corporate operationalisation of a contested con-
cept, and its scores were used simultaneously as
an evaluation target and an evaluation standard.
Its closure leaves behind non-updatable bench-
marks, irreproducible results, and ultimately a
field at risk of perpetuating these issues by turn-
ing to closed-source LLMs. We use PERSPEC-
TIVE’s announced termination as an opportu-
nity to call for an independent, valid, adaptable,
and reproducible toxicity and hate speech mea-
surement infrastructure, with the technical and
governance requirements outlined in this paper.
1
Introduction
Online abuse can have profound real-world conse-
quences, including the suppression of marginalised
voices, deterioration of mental health, and violence
against marginalised groups (Matsuda et al., 1993;
Marques, 2023; Luther et al., 2025). To address
this challenge, a substantial body of research has
focused on developing automated classifiers to de-
tect such content at scale (Vidgen and Derczyn-
ski, 2020). One classification tool has emerged as
particularly influential, namely PERSPECTIVE API,
developed by Google’s technology incubator Jig-
saw. Since 2017, it has provided a free and scalable
API for classifying toxicity, an umbrella term for
harmful content. Its widespread adoption has led to
it being described as “a cornerstone for academic
research on online abuse and incivility” (Nogara
et al., 2025).
Despite its popularity, Jigsaw recently an-
nounced that PERSPECTIVE API will cease opera-
tion at the end of 2026. The sunset announcement
celebrates a decade of impact, stating that the sys-
tem has “grown from an experimental tool into
a helpful solution for publishers and platforms”.
However, the tool and infrastructure are to be shut
down because, “[a]s AI capabilities evolve, [Jigsaw
is] setting [its] sights on new challenges”.1 For
research communities that have built their work
around PERSPECTIVE API, this discontinuation rep-
resents a sudden withdrawal of critical infrastruc-
ture, exposing the field’s dependence on a propri-
etary, externally controlled measurement tool.
We argue that the closure is not a tooling prob-
lem, but a measurement problem: The field built
its toxicity research on a tool it neither owned, nor
versioned, nor validated for most of the ways it
was used. Therefore, the response is not to find
a drop-in replacement, but to rebuild the condi-
tions for valid, reliable, and reproducible toxicity
measurement. The paper develops this argument
in four steps. We first trace how PERSPECTIVE
API was used across natural language processing
(NLP), computational social science (CSS), and
large language model (LLM) evaluation research
and what drove its adoption (§2). We then show
that, judged against standard procedures of mea-
surement validation, the tool was never fit for the
central role it came to play, with consequences for
validity, reliability, and reproducibility (§3). Build-
ing on this analysis, we propose five technical and
five governance requirements for an independent
successor infrastructure (§4). Finally, we reflect
on the role of researchers in content moderation,
toxicity research, and LLM evaluation (§5).

2
PERSPECTIVE API and Its Research
Uptake
2.1
Use in Research
Within academic research, PERSPECTIVE API was
taken up across communities in two distinct ways
(Figure 1 demonstrates the latter use): as a subject
of evaluation and as a tool for evaluation.
Perspective as a baseline model
In toxicity and
hate speech detection research, PERSPECTIVE API
was primarily treated as a system to be evaluated.
It served as a reference point in benchmark studies,
where its toxicity scores were used to assess classi-
fication performance relative to other models. For
example, HateCheck (Röttger et al., 2021) includes
PERSPECTIVE API among the evaluated systems,
positioning it as one model within a broader land-
scape of toxicity detection approaches.
Perspective as a measurement tool
In contrast,
CSS and LLM evaluation research primarily used
PERSPECTIVE API as a tool to measure toxicity at
scale. In CSS, researchers applied the API in large-
scale studies of online discourse (e.g., Frimer et al.,
2023; Kim et al., 2021; Theocharis et al., 2020;
Chang et al., 2023; Mosleh et al., 2024; Gervais
et al., 2025). In LLM evaluation (benchmarking,
auditing, and red teaming), PERSPECTIVE API was
embedded into evaluation operationalisations to
label model outputs and for red teaming to label po-
tential offensive model inputs (e.g., Gehman et al.,
2020; Liu et al., 2021; Liang et al., 2023; Gallegos
et al., 2024; Welbl et al., 2021; Perez et al., 2022;
Lee et al., 2023).
2.2
Drivers of Adoption
At its peak, PERSPECTIVE API processed 500 mil-
lion requests daily (Jigsaw, 2021), and was inte-
grated into comment systems at major publishers,
including the New York Times, Vox Media, and
OpenWeb (Rieder and Skop, 2021; Jigsaw, 2021),
while also becoming widely adopted in academic
research (Ribeiro, 2024). In what follows, we ex-
amine the factors behind this widespread adoption.
Timing
PERSPECTIVE’s launch in 2017 followed
a surge in online abuse, including high-profile ha-
rassment campaigns, the spread of conspiratorial
narratives (Venturini, 2019), inter-ethnic violence
and genocide (Mozur, 2018), and the mobilisation
of political extremism online (Ganesh and Bright,
2020). This surge put increasing pressure on plat-
forms to act. For instance, Germany’s Network En-
forcement Act (NetzDG), passed in 2017, followed
a wave of anti-refugee hate speech and required


platforms to remove clearly illegal content. As
Gorwa (2019) documents, this pressure contributed
to an institutional shift from user-driven flagging
to platform-centred moderation infrastructures, in-
cluding automated or semi-automated moderation
(see also Myers West, 2018; Gorwa et al., 2020).
This context also motivated early work on auto-
matic hate speech detection (Waseem and Hovy,
2016), laying foundations for computational mod-
eration tools. PERSPECTIVE thus emerged at the
intersection of regulatory pressure and a nascent
research field, providing a scalable moderation so-
lution (Davidson et al., 2017) as human modera-
tion became increasingly infeasible (Gorwa et al.,
2020).
Cost and access
Another reason for adoption is
that using PERSPECTIVE API was free, whereas
competing tools, such as AMAZON REKOGNITION,
charged per query (Estha, 2024). Access was pro-
vided upon application to Jigsaw, though accep-
tance criteria remained opaque (Rieder and Skop,
2021). For accepted clients, the API offered a
100ms response time and an expandable quota on
request, making large-scale studies and automated
moderation feasible at no cost. Its multilingual cov-
erage across 18 languages, trained on 38 million
records (Lees et al., 2022), further enabled research
beyond English in a field largely dominated by En-
glish resources (Tonneau et al., 2024).
Ease of use and transparency
PERSPECTIVE
API’s ease of use reinforced these advantages. It
accepted single-sentence inputs without preprocess-
ing and returned an easily interpretable scalar score,
lowering the barrier to integration in both research
and production systems. In addition, Jigsaw pro-
vided model cards, threshold guidance, and partial
architectural documentation via GitHub (Jigsaw,
2022), offering a level of transparency uncommon
among commercial APIs (Hartmann et al., 2025b).
The team further engaged with the research com-
munity through peer-reviewed publications, bench-
mark datasets (Dixon et al., 2018; Lees et al., 2022),
and direct responses to researcher feedback (Jig-
saw, 2023). While this documentation was not com-
prehensive in all respects, as we detail in the next
section, it nonetheless positioned PERSPECTIVE
API as a comparatively transparent and research-
embedded proprietary tool.
Path dependence and network effects
As Star
(1999) argues, tools become infrastructure through
their embeddedness in practice. Once a measure-
ment instrument is taken up across a field, it begins
to shape what is measurable, comparable, and cred-
ible, thereby generating path dependence (Bowker
and Star, 1999). We argue that PERSPECTIVE API
exemplifies this dynamic: its integration into NLP
benchmarking suites such as RealToxicityPrompts
(Gehman et al., 2020) and the Holistic Evaluation
of Language Models (HELM) (Liang et al., 2023),
as well as its use in CSS studies of political incivil-
ity and online harassment (Theocharis et al., 2020;
Gervais et al., 2025), positioned it as a common
reference point across research contexts. This stan-
dardisation enabled comparability across studies,
which in turn encouraged continued use, creating a
self-reinforcing dynamic consistent with network
effects (Katz and Shapiro, 1994). In this sense,
PERSPECTIVE API was not necessarily adopted be-
cause it was the most valid or best-performing tool,
but because it had become an established point of
reference, effectively positioning it over time as the
de facto standard for toxicity detection.
3
Was PERSPECTIVE API Ever Fit for
Purpose? A Measure Development
Pipeline and Infrastructural Critique
Becoming a standard through path dependence and
network effects is not the same as being validated
as one. In this section, we assess whether PER-
SPECTIVE API was fit for the central role it came
to play in research by comparing its development
to established procedures of measurement valida-
tion in the social sciences (Clark and Watson, 2019;
Jacobs and Wallach, 2021; Wallach et al., 2024).
In this tradition, a concept (i.e., a broad and often
contested notion) is first systematised into a con-
struct (i.e., a more specific and explicitly defined
understanding), specifying what is to be measured
(Adcock and Collier, 2001). The construct is then
operationalised through a measurement instrument,
specifying how it is to be measured. Both steps,
(1) from concept to construct through systematisa-
tion and (2) from construct to measurement instru-
ment through operationalisation, are inherently
situated and involve analytical choices (Wallach
et al., 2024). They rely on assumptions that must
be made explicit and supported theoretically and
empirically.2
2This is commonly referred to as construct validation, the
process of establishing whether a measurement instrument
captures what it is intended to measure or, in other words, of
providing theoretical and evidential support for one’s opera-


Here, we show that PERSPECTIVE API provides
limited grounding for key assumptions in both its
systematisation (§3.1) and operationalisation and
provision of the measurement infrastructure (§3.2),
and that these limitations have implications for per-
formance and research use (§3.3). We further iden-
tify structural issues in its application, particularly
in cases where it is used to both define and measure
toxicity (§3.4).
3.1
Systematisation
Contested Behavioural Assumption
PERSPEC-
TIVE API’s construct of toxicity rests on a be-
havioural assumption that is empirically contested.
Jigsaw defines toxicity as “a rude, disrespectful, or
unreasonable comment that is likely to make peo-
ple leave a discussion” (Dixon et al., 2018; Rieder
and Skop, 2021), thereby tying toxicity to disen-
gagement. However, empirical evidence suggests
that this effect is not stable. For example, Beknazar-
Yuzbashev et al. (2025) show that removing toxic
content from social media feeds causally reduces
time spent, ad impressions, and content consump-
tion, indicating that its presence contributes to user
engagement. Observationally, out-group animosity
is the strongest predictor of shares and retweets on
Facebook and Twitter (Rathje et al., 2021), and
toxic conversations on Twitter tend to generate
larger, wider, and deeper reply trees than non-toxic
ones (Saveski et al., 2021). Taken together, this
evidence challenges the disengagement premise:
the same toxic content can repel some readers and
engage others, depending on their relationship to
it. A construct that ties toxicity to a single, univer-
sal behavioural effect, therefore mistakes a reader-
dependent phenomenon for a property of the text.
Insufficiently Specified Construct
Even beyond
this contested behavioural assumption, the con-
struct remains insufficiently specified. PERSPEC-
TIVE API provides scores for multiple “toxic at-
tributes”, including threat, insult, identity attack,
severe toxicity, and profanity, suggesting a decom-
position of toxicity into subcomponents. However,
Jigsaw provides only brief, one-sentence defini-
tions of these attributes and does not clearly dis-
tinguish between them, explain how they relate
to the overarching toxicity construct, specify how
they should be used in practice, or indicate whether
this set of attributes is intended to be exhaustive
(Rieder and Skop, 2021; Hartmann et al., 2025b).
tionalisation (Cronbach and Meehl, 1955).
As a result, both the scope of the construct and the
relationship between the overall construct and its
purported subcomponents remain unclear. Without
a well-specified construct, it is difficult to deter-
mine what exactly is being measured, or to assess
its validity (Wallach et al., 2024).
Construct-Measure Mismatch
This lack of
specification enables a mismatch between the in-
tended construct and its use in downstream re-
search, particularly in studies of hate speech. Toxic-
ity and hate speech are related but distinct concepts
(Barth et al., 2023): while toxicity encompasses
rude or unreasonable language more generally, hate
speech involves discriminatory acts targeting indi-
viduals or groups based on protected characteristics
(Dixon et al., 2018; Marques, 2023). A measure-
ment instrument designed for toxicity therefore
cannot be assumed to validly capture hate speech.
We observe three recurring usage patterns in the
literature. The first uses the toxicity score to mea-
sure toxic language, aligning with the tool’s in-
tended use, though constrained by its behavioural
definition.
The second uses attributes such as
IDENTITY_ATTACK as proxies for hate speech, typ-
ically acknowledging the construct gap explicitly
(e.g., Tonneau et al. (2025)). The third frames re-
search questions in terms of hate speech, political
incivility, or LLM safety and operationalises them
using the toxicity score without acknowledging the
lack of theoretical alignment (Gervais et al., 2025;
Gehman et al., 2020). This last pattern is particu-
larly problematic, as the measurement instrument
does not match the target construct and the mis-
match is not made explicit.
3.2
Operationalisation and Provision
Having examined how toxicity is conceptualised,
we now analyse how it is operationalised and pro-
visioned in the evaluation tool PERSPECTIVE API.
We focus on three aspects: the input representa-
tion, the model and its provision, and the resulting
outputs.
Input: Context-free
PERSPECTIVE API takes a
single sentence or short text as input and returns
a toxicity score, thereby operationalising toxicity
as a property identifiable in isolated text (Rieder
and Skop, 2021; Hartmann et al., 2025b). However,
the meaning of a sentence depends on its conversa-
tional context, community norms, who is speaking,
who is targeted, and the relationship between speak-
ers and receivers (Anderson and Barnes, 2023; Yo-


der et al., 2022; Mosca et al., 2021). By design,
PERSPECTIVE API strips this context away, lim-
iting the measurement instrument to surface tex-
tual features and excluding the contextual and re-
lational dimensions that define toxicity as a social
phenomenon. As a result, the same text receives
the same score across contexts, even though its per-
ceived toxicity depends on context-specific norms,
making the resulting scores difficult to interpret.
Model: Misaligned and Opaque
The model un-
derlying PERSPECTIVE API is misaligned with its
published specification and lacks sufficient trans-
parency, limiting users’ ability to assess what it
measures. Most consequentially, the annotation
scheme used to generate training labels, while par-
tially available (Conversation AI, 2017), diverges
from Jigsaw’s public definition of toxicity (Dixon
et al., 2018; Rieder and Skop, 2021). Whereas the
public definition frames toxicity as a conjunctive
criterion, namely a rude or disrespectful comment
that is likely to make users leave a discussion, the
annotation scheme applies these criteria disjunc-
tively, allowing labels to be assigned based on rude-
ness or anticipated behavioural effects alone. As
a result, the model is trained on labels that do not
correspond to the definition users are given, creat-
ing a gap between construct and operationalisation.
This issue is compounded by a lack of transparency
about the annotation process, including annotator
demographics, data sources, and labelling proce-
dures (Hartmann et al., 2025b; Rieder and Skop,
2021). Adding another layer of opacity, Pozzobon
et al. (2023) document that the underlying model of
the PERSPECTIVE API was silently retrained over
time without version pinning, changelogs, or public
disclosure, except for a Google group where they
announced changes.
Output: Uncalibrated
The outputs of PERSPEC-
TIVE API are not calibrated to any interpretable
real-world quantity. The API returns a score be-
tween 0 and 1, but this score does not correspond
to prevalence, severity, or annotator agreement.
According to Jigsaw’s technical documentation,
scores are normalised against a balanced 50/50
toxic and non-toxic dataset rather than any real-
world distribution (Lees et al., 2022), meaning
they reflect model confidence relative to an arti-
ficial baseline (Nogara et al., 2025) rather than the
prevalence of harm. Although Jigsaw and exter-
nal researchers provided some threshold guidance
(Hua et al., 2020a,b), these offer no principled ba-
sis for selecting thresholds that correspond to in-
terpretable quantities, leaving threshold-setting as
an implicit design decision made by individual re-
searchers (Hartmann et al., 2025b). As a result,
scores lack a stable interpretation and depend on ar-
bitrary and often unreported thresholding choices.
3.3
Consequences for Research Quality
The limitations in systematisation and operational-
isation outlined above translate into measurable
problems for research quality. As PERSPECTIVE
API became widely embedded in research work-
flows, these limitations produced systematic errors,
inconsistent results, and biases across use cases.
Lacking Validity and Performance
Construct
validity issues translate into poor classification per-
formance when PERSPECTIVE API is applied be-
yond its intended scope. Gervais et al. (2025) show
that PERSPECTIVE scores on congressional tweets
achieve a maximum F1 of 0.33 against human-
coded political incivility across all decision thresh-
olds, and Mihaljevi´c and Steffen (2022) find that
it detects antisemitism only at a very basic level.
These failures are particularly pronounced where
interpretation depends on context. In such cases,
the model systematically misclassifies meaning:
counterspeech is labelled as hateful when speaker
intent is not considered (Gligori´c et al., 2024), re-
claimed slurs are over-moderated when community
membership is unavailable (Hartmann et al., 2025b;
Röttger et al., 2021), and implicit hate speech,
which relies on background knowledge, is system-
atically missed (Hartmann et al., 2025b).
Undermined Reliability and Reproducibility
The lack of model versioning undermines the re-
liability and reproducibility of results. Because
toxicity is a dynamic concept, with slurs evolv-
ing and new forms of expression emerging (Siegel,
2020; Mendelsohn et al., 2023), the absence of ver-
sioning means that PERSPECTIVE API effectively
functions as a moving target, making it impossi-
ble to determine whether repeated queries refer
to the same measurement instrument. Pozzobon
et al. (2023) show that 49% of previously toxic
prompts were classified differently upon rescor-
ing, and HELM rankings were inverted. This in-
dicates that researchers were effectively querying
a changing system, and because model updates
were neither documented nor versioned, it is not
possible to determine whether results obtained at
different points in time are comparable. The shut-


down makes this problem permanent: scores can
no longer be recovered or verified, rendering PER-
SPECTIVE API-based benchmarks irreproducible.
Systematic Bias and Limited Attribution
Sys-
tematic bias is evident in the outputs of PERSPEC-
TIVE API, but its sources cannot be fully attributed
due to limited transparency in the underlying data
and annotation processes. Independent audits show
a consistent pattern of over-moderation of identity-
related content alongside under-detection of im-
plicit hate speech. For example, content associated
with LGBTQIA+ communities and reclaimed slurs
is disproportionately flagged as toxic (Dias Oliva
et al., 2021; Röttger et al., 2021), while hate di-
rected at marginalised groups, in general, is often
underdetected (Hartmann et al., 2025b). These
patterns are consistent with a reliance on surface
features such as identity terms and the use of
context-free inputs. Biases also extend across lan-
guages and regions: Nogara et al. (2025) show that
German-language text is rated as more toxic than
comparable content in other languages, and cross-
geographic disparities in toxicity detection perfor-
mance are well documented (Ghosh et al., 2021).
Such disparities align with prior work showing that
annotator demographics, beliefs, and annotation
guidelines shape what is labelled as toxic in edge
cases (Sap et al., 2022; Davani et al., 2023). How-
ever, because key aspects of the annotation process
remain only partially documented, including anno-
tator composition and labelling procedures, these
biases cannot be systematically evaluated, com-
pared, or corrected by downstream users.
3.4
Structural Circularity: When the
Measure Becomes the Standard
These problems do not remain confined to indi-
vidual studies but accumulate at the level of the
research network, producing a structural circularity.
Because PERSPECTIVE API provided an accessible
and scalable source of toxicity scores, it came to
function not only as a measurement tool but also
as a source of training data and an evaluation stan-
dard. The same system that generated labels was
also used to evaluate models, creating the condi-
tions for a self-reinforcing loop that runs through
the field’s most influential resources, including Re-
alToxicityPrompts and the benchmarks built on it
(Gehman et al., 2020; Pozzobon et al., 2023).
This dynamic emerges across the literature in
three recurring steps. First, because large-scale
human annotation is expensive and the API is
readily accessible, researchers used PERSPECTIVE
scores to generate training labels for toxicity and
hate speech datasets (Gehman et al., 2020). Sec-
ond, models trained on these labels were evalu-
ated against PERSPECTIVE outputs, either directly
through score correlation or indirectly through
benchmarks whose gold labels were themselves
generated using the API (Gehman et al., 2020; Poz-
zobon et al., 2023). Third, models that achieved
high agreement with PERSPECTIVE were reported
as performing well at toxicity or hate speech detec-
tion (Pavlopoulos et al., 2019). At each step, re-
searchers converted uncalibrated continuous scores
into binary labels by applying an ad hoc thresh-
old such as t = 0.7 (see stage ➂in Figure 1) and
treated these derived labels as ground truth, de-
spite lacking a principled interpretation. Threshold
choices were often not reported, and the meaning
of the scores remained unspecified (Pozzobon et al.,
2023; Hartmann et al., 2025b).
What was ultimately being measured, however,
was not toxicity, but conformity to a single sys-
tem’s decision threshold. This threshold reflects
a specific platform, annotator pool, cultural con-
text, and point in time, normalised against an artifi-
cial baseline rather than any real-world distribution
(Lees et al., 2022), without an explicit specification
of what toxicity means for whom (Wallach et al.,
2024; Jacobs and Wallach, 2021; Blodgett et al.,
2021). Because training and evaluation rely on the
same system, systematic errors become embedded
in the evaluation criterion and thus remain invisible.
Models inheriting PERSPECTIVE’s biases, includ-
ing over-moderation of dialects, reclaimed slurs, or
content related to marginalised groups (Dias Oliva
et al., 2021; Hartmann et al., 2025b), will perform
well on PERSPECTIVE-derived benchmarks, since
these errors are encoded in the standard itself. As
Blodgett et al. (2020) argue, when underlying so-
cial assumptions are not made explicit, they are
laundered through technical framing until they ap-
pear neutral. Circular evaluation is one mechanism
through which this laundering occurs.
Once PERSPECTIVE API became the measure, it
ceased to function as one (Strathern, 1997). Un-
derstanding why the field arrived at this point re-
quires situating this technical dependence within
the broader platform-governance context in which
the tool was built and ultimately abandoned. We
turn to this next, followed by recommendations
based on these critiques.

Validity
Evaluation tools should explicitly document which constructs, con-
ditions, and input formats it measures, including limitations such as
threshold selection and out-of-scope queries (Wallach et al., 2024;
Jacobs and Wallach, 2021; Blodgett et al., 2021).
Construct underspeci-
fication
T3
Contextuality
Scoring should support structured metadata input–sender, target, and
prior context–to enable classification of counterspeech and reclaimed
language (Yu et al., 2022).
Misclassification
of
identity-laden content
T4
Uncertainty
Evaluation tools should return a full probability distribution over
labels rather than a point estimate, as annotator disagreement reflects
contested constructs (Leonardelli et al., 2021; Uma et al., 2022).
Omitted annotator dis-
agreement
T5
Multilinguality
Performance must be validated and documented per language, with
explicit disclosure where it falls below a defined threshold (Nogara
et al., 2025; Tonneau et al., 2025).
Uneven cross-lingual
performance
G1
Independence
The infrastructure should be open-source and institutionally inde-
pendent of any commercial entity, so no single organisation controls
annotation schema, model weights, or the definition of toxicity, as
PERSPECTIVE API demonstrated (Rieder and Skop, 2021; Pozzobon
et al., 2023).
Single-vendor depen-
dence
G2
Transparency
Model weights, training data, and annotation schemata should be
open and auditable, including annotator demographics, which influ-
ence group-level disparities (Sap et al., 2022; Davani et al., 2023;
Kraft et al., 2025).
Opacity of training
and annotation
G3
Legitimacy
Defining toxicity, selecting communities, and collecting training data
must involve affected communities through an open, documented
process (Maronikolakis et al., 2022).
Circular,
self-
validating evaluation
G4
Accountability
Auditing with published results and documented remediation across
demographic groups, languages, and content types should be a con-
tinuous, open process (Garg et al., 2023; Hartmann et al., 2026).
Undetected systematic
errors
G5
Sustainability
A long-term funding model must be put in place that does not repro-
duce the single-funder dependence that made PERSPECTIVE API’s
shutdown so disruptive (Rieder and Skop, 2021).

4
What Now? Towards Independent
Research Infrastructure
The decision to discontinue PERSPECTIVE API at
this moment cannot be understood without the
broader shift in the platform governance landscape.
Since 2024, major platforms have reduced modera-
tion workforces (McMahon et al., 2025; McGuirk,
2024; Gerken, 2025), loosened content rules (Bid-
dle, 2025), curtailed researcher data access (Burnat
and Davidson, 2025; Hartmann et al., 2025a), and
dismantled trust and safety teams more broadly
(Moran et al., 2025). Whether one reads these
moves as a withdrawal from earlier moderation
commitments (Magalhães et al., 2026) or as a more
pragmatic recalibration, their cumulative effect is
the same: the institutional support that underwrote
a tool like PERSPECTIVE API is weaker than it
was a decade ago. The underlying problem has
not diminished. Toxic speech appears to be rising
on several major platforms (Törnberg and Chueri,
2025; Hickey et al., 2025) even as already weak
and inconsistent enforcement (Tonneau et al., 2026)
is further scaled back, and online toxicity contin-
ues to be implicated in offline violence, including
anti-migrant riots from the UK (Venkataramakrish-
nan, 2025; CNN, 2025) to Spain (Euronews, 2025).
Any commercial infrastructure successor faces the
same vulnerability, and without an alternative, re-
searchers will turn to the next proprietary tool.


Do not repeat the mistake
Besides the afore-
mentioned risks imposed by the absence of PER-
SPECTIVE API, its replacement with something sim-
ilar or worse should be of concern. Closed-source
LLM endpoints are already used as toxicity clas-
sifiers in evaluation pipelines, subject to the same
silent model updates, construct underspecification,
and political exposure, but without model cards,
threshold guidance, or a research-facing team. The
OPENAI MODERATION ENDPOINT, for example,
although performing even better than PERSPEC-
TIVE API for some target groups, has very limited
transparency regarding its training, updating, or an-
notation schema (Hartmann et al., 2025b). On top
of that, OPENAI’s toxicity classifiers are known
to have been trained on labels produced under ex-
ploitative conditions (Perrigo, 2023). Outsourc-
ing toxicity measurement to entities with active
interests in its definition is not a neutral technical
choice.
Immediate actions
Before the shutdown on 31
December 2026, the community should archive
PERSPECTIVE scores for all major benchmarks
with full method documentation, including query
date, threshold settings, and API version where re-
trievable. Papers relying on PERSPECTIVE scores
should register them as versioned data artefacts.
For new projects, open-weight models with ex-
plicit versioning should be preferred over closed
endpoints, and any use of generative LLMs as clas-
sifiers must disclose all parameters and system
prompts in full.
Requirements and recommendations
Drawing
on the limitations documented in Section 3, Table 1
proposes ten requirements for a successor measure-
ment infrastructure. These fall into two groups.
The technical requirements address core measure-
ment failures, including reproducibility, construct
validity, contextuality, uncertainty, and multilin-
gual performance. The governance requirements
address the structural conditions under which these
failures emerged, including dependence on a sin-
gle provider, limited transparency, lack of legit-
imacy in construct definition, weak accountabil-
ity mechanisms, and funding fragility. Together,
these requirements define the minimum conditions
under which toxicity measurement can be consid-
ered valid, reliable, and fair. We treat them not as
desiderata but as preconditions for legitimate mea-
surement and call for their joint implementation in
future infrastructure.
5
Concluding Remarks
The closure of PERSPECTIVE API is an opportunity
for researchers to be honest about their own role
in establishing and sustaining the dependence dis-
cussed in this paper. The community was not a pas-
sive part within a fragile infrastructure. It adopted
a corporate tool, incorporated it into benchmark
suites, declared it a standard measure, and even
continued using it after its validity problems were
known and published. The latter was demonstrated
in the case of Holistic Evaluation of Language
Models (HELM), where the limitations of using
PERSPECTIVE API were even acknowledged but
ignored for purposes of comparability. Understand-
ing why this happened and why no alternative tool
was built or even proposed is as much a question
about our epistemic practices as it is about our tech-
nical innovation processes. The most immediate
action researchers can take now is to stop treat-
ing measurement infrastructure as someone else’s
problem and take accountability. With this call
for reflexivity and accountability, we are joining
the active debate in the field of critical research on
dataset creation and use (Paullada et al., 2021; Sam-
basivan et al., 2021), while extending it to the mea-
surement infrastructure that relies on and shapes
those datasets. The community needs to treat the
construction of measurement infrastructure as a re-
search contribution in its own right and as a form
of care. Annotation schemas, inter-rater reliability
scores, dataset construction decisions, and calibra-
tion evaluations deserve the same methodological
rigour and visibility as model performance results.
The field has the capacity to build the infrastruc-
ture it needs.
The datasets exist as starting points,
and the techniques for uncertainty quantification,
per-concept fine-tuning, and context-aware classifi-
cation are not unresolved problems (see Table 1).
What has been missing is the collective decision to
treat infrastructure-building as scientifically valu-
able work rather than service labour. Funding bod-
ies, programme committees, and tenure committees
all participate in that decision, and the community
can make strategic choices to change how such con-
tributions are recognised and rewarded. A jointly
maintained, community-governed classifier system
is not utopian. It is the kind of shared task infras-
tructure the NLP community has built before, and
it is within reach if the field decides to prioritise it.

Abstract: The closure of PERSPECTIVE API at the end of 2026 discards what has functioned as the de facto standard for automated toxicity mea- surement in NLP, CSS, and LLM evaluation re- search. We document the structural dependence that the communities built on this single pro- prietary tool and discuss how this dependence caused epistemic problems that have affected— and will likely continue to affect—collective research efforts. PERSPECTIVE’s model was pe- riodically updated without versioning or disclo- sure, its annotation structure reflected a single corporate operationalisation of a contested con- cept, and its scores were used simultaneously as an evaluation target and an evaluation standard. Its closure leaves behind non-updatable bench- marks, irreproducible results, and ultimately a field at risk of perpetuating these issues by turn- ing to closed-source LLMs. We use PERSPEC- TIVE’s announced termination as an opportu- nity to call for an independent, valid, adaptable, and reproducible toxicity and hate speech mea- surement infrastructure, with the technical and governance requirements outlined in this paper.
